developments: Ranked by what the accepted set supports. (1) Proactive personal agents with account access, led by Meta's Muse, moved into everyday use. The evidence is Mollick's first-hand cases, the Muse designer's account, Vergecast hands-on use, and first-hand failures (the Muse doctor-number mix-up; the Grokbot Slack leak, which is relayed only). (2) OS- and device-level assistants built on personal context shipped in beta or first-generation form: Siri AI beta (NN/g test), Apple HomeView with face-based user switching (MKBHD, Vergecast), and Googlebook with OS-level Gemini (MKBHD, Google roundup). (3) Agent infrastructure arrived on the desktop and in the cloud: Microsoft's MXC containment is generally available, while Copilot local actions are still promised (Microsoft, Witteveen). Gemini's chat-to-tasks toggle and 40+ connectors have shipped to paying users (Google). (4) Computer-use models are converging on 'GUI as last resort' (Holo4, Muse Wonder computer-use test). Holding against all of this is independent evidence on oversight: undetected agent errors (arXiv delegation study), the cost of maintaining context (NN/g), voice-AI persuasion and sycophancy (arXiv), and chat failing without domain vocabulary (Plottery).
missing_perspectives: Users outside tech: almost all evidence comes from experts, reviewers, developers or professionals, and the voice study is the only general-public sample (UK). Missing as well are accessibility users, non-US and non-English users, and privacy advocates or regulators commenting on agents with account access and always-on home cameras. No eligible item gives usable evidence on smart glasses or wearables; the only glasses item is a storage accessory, so the personal-context theme lacks wearable coverage and this must be stated in that piece's limitations. There is no independent test of Gemini tasks mode, Gemini Spark on Windows or Copilot local actions (the last has not shipped). The Alexa Plus assessment and the JPMorgan agent-blocking remark are relayed only. No longitudinal or adoption data exists beyond vendor and commentator claims, and generative-UI evidence is limited to a vendor's design account and a brief widget note.
balance: The accepted set has 21 items from 12 publishers, mixing vendor (Google x3, Microsoft x1), independent journalism and reviews (Vergecast x2, MKBHD x2, Big Technology x1), practitioners (NN/g, Claire Vo x3, Sam Witteveen x2, Mollick x2) and research (arXiv x3). All formats contribute: written (arXiv, NN/g, Google, Microsoft, Mollick), video (MKBHD, Witteveen) and podcast (Vergecast, Big Technology, How I AI). Each piece has more than three independent publishers. Piece 01: Mollick, Google, Microsoft, NN/g, Vo, Verge, MKBHD, Witteveen. Piece 02: arXiv, Mollick, Google, NN/g, Big Technology, Vo, Verge, MKBHD, Witteveen. Piece 03: arXiv, Mollick, Microsoft, NN/g, Big Technology, Vo, Verge, Witteveen. Theme coverage: agents and personal context are strong. Voice and conversational interfaces are covered through the voice persuasion study, Plottery, Rambler and the HomeView voice-recognition gap, though the voice-specific evidence is thinner. OS and device AI is well covered, and wearables and glasses are uncovered. Muse is over-represented across sources, so vendor claims about it must be attributed and set against the failure anecdotes.
